Initially, the temperature field is solved without considering radiation. Then a tentative radiational heat flux is calculated based on the initial solved temperature field. After that, this tentative radiational heat flux is included to update the temperature field. If the difference between the updated temperature field and previous solved temperature field is small enough, we would assume the model converges. A code workflow is included in Fig. 2. Fig. 2: Thermal model code workflow The thermal boundary conditions for the coupled model are set as follows: temperature at all out boundary except the top boundary is set to be 293.15 K the Page 7 of 30 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. top boundary is insulated (no heat flux crosses it), the inlet gas temperature is 293.15 K and the temperature at the neck surface of the boule is 1673.15. This is the melting temperature of silicon, a temperature which is obviously required to get the polycrystalline material to melt and flow for recrystallization during the float zone process. For the flow simulation, the velocity boundary condition at the inlet of gas is calculated based on the flow rate of each species, which is 0.0078 m/s for HSiCl 3 and 0.011 m/s for Ar and the pressure at the outlet is set to be 0. The simulated radiational heat flux (positive value means it absorb radiational heat flux which is flipped from the preliminary simulation) on the growth surface is shown in Fig. 3(a) while Fig.3(b) shows that on reactor surfaces. Based on Fig. 3, one can tell the boule releases while the reactor absorbs heat flux through radiation as the boule surface is much hotter. It is obvious that the radiation heat transfer decreases the temperature on the boule surface. In addition, as the bottom boule surface is where the silicon is deposited, understanding its temperature is more critical. Fig. 5 shows the temperature distribution on the bottom boule surface, where the Si vapor deposition reaction will occur, without (a) and with (b) radiation.
